highlights.summary: Meta now lets you make your own Muse gadgets that feature the company's new AI agent with code that the company open sourced. The company suggests projects like loading Muse on a color E Ink display to show reminders, adding it to an HDMI stick so you can display Muse on a big screen, or putting…
body: Meta now lets you connect Muse to your own hardware to put on your displays or a Raspberry Pi.

“Muse gadgets are open source devices you build yourself,” Meta says. “Program an off-the-shelf ESP32 board or set up a Raspberry Pi with our SDKs, then connect Muse to your displays, buttons, sensors, actuators, and whatever else you’ve got lying on your workbench.” However, Meta cautions that you should “Proceed at your own risk!”

The company is also giving away a Muse Home Link gadget that it created. With the Muse Home Link, you use community-built skills to have the AI agent “turn on a light, control your TV, send a document to a printer, and more, depending on your setup,” Meta says. It manufactured 5,000 of the gadgets, according to Meta Superintelligence Labs’ Nat Friedman, and you can claim a waitlist spot for the Muse Home Link now ahead of shipping sometime this month.

highlights.summary: Max Verstappen claimed Red Bull's first pole position of the season as he beat Lewis Hamilton in qualifying for the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.
body: Verstappen and Hamilton will share the front row in Sunday's race at 8am (build-up from 6.30am), live on Sky Sports F1 and Main Event, for the first time since Hungary 2023 after the Red Bull driver delivered a dominant qualifying performance.
The Dutchman topped each segment of qualifying and set two laps good enough for pole, ending up 0.298s faster than Hamilton.
Isack Hadjar equalled his best career qualifying result with third but will start eighth due to a five-grid place penalty for a new internal combustion engine.
Championship leader Kimi Antonelli will start third after a costly mistake in Q2 forced him to use an extra set of tyres prior to Q3, leaving him with just one run in the final part of qualifying.

highlights.title: "We felt that fans were getting a bit desensitised to the violence" Gears of War: E-Day devs made a "big investment" in gore, and weirdly, it works
highlights.summary: Buoyed by some commendatory early reviews and fantastic initial player numbers, Gears of War: E-Day has found a solid audience a weekend before general release. And a large part of its appeal is the combat; I noted in my review I think it's the tightest Gears has ever been, augmented by some…
body: And it turns out there's a lot more intricate thought behind this eruption of violence than perhaps people realise, as I discovered in an interview with Coalition studio art director Aryan Hanbeck, brand director Nicole Fawcett, and creative director Matt Searcy.

"Think about getting a headshot, right, a really good headshot," says Hanbeck. "A lot of work goes into that moment, into what happens on the screen when you take a headshot. There's an audio component to that, too, as well as all the effects - how high the blood spurts go, how much mist we leave behind, what the body does afterwards… So, it's not just the weapon itself, it's what you see and hear when you do what it's supposed to do, or when you get up close and you melee with [your Lancer or Breechshot] or execute an enemy, which is really cool."
"And there's a big investment in gore in this game," adds Searcy. "That's a huge aspect of [what makes combat so satisfying]."

highlights.summary: Many major mobile game makers are giving a percentage of their UK revenue to disability charity Special Effect today, Friday October 2. body: A slice of player spend from games including Clash of Clans, Brawl Stars, Clash Royale, Angry Birds 2, Golf Clash, Subway Surfers, Dream League Soccer, 8 Ball Pool and more will be donated to Special Effect for today only. A full list of participating games is available via the One Special Day site.

Special Effect provides assessments and customised technology loans to help physically disabled people play games, and takes what it learns back to hardware and software developers to help make their products more accessible. Thousands of disabled people ask for the charity’s help every year.

“We’ve been proud to partner with Special Effect across our games for nearly a decade, and that relationship has grown far beyond One Special Day,” said Supercell’s Deborah Mensah-Bonsu. “From cycling in Helsinki and joining One Special Walk in London, to learning from their incredible work as we think more deeply about inclusive design, we’re continually inspired by their tenacity, generosity and tremendous heart, and by how they show the games industry can genuinely change lives for the better.”

The year is unspecified, but the fatigued brutalist housing blocks of outer Bucharest are still standing: Though it doesn’t specify a location either, “April X” uses the present-day wear and tear of the Romanian capital, where the film was shot on location, as shorthand for a world collapsing into concrete ruin. The odd hi-tech drone adds some futuristic pizzazz to the film’s exterior vistas, but the new technologies defining the narrative aren’t of the gleaming, brave-new-world variety: People are being cloned in grubby, shadowed fashion, while memories and dreams can be captured and downloaded onto surprisingly retro-looking data devices.

highlights.title: A Decade-Long Experiment Is Unlocking the Mysteries of the Ocean’s ‘Deep Reefs’
highlights.summary: Scientists left structures up to 100 meters under the surface. Here’s what they found when they retrieved them 10 years later.
body: This story originally appeared on Vox and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

On a bright, sunny day last May, I stood on a boat surrounded by the turquoise waters of the island nation of Palau. I was there in the western Pacific watching scuba divers as they prepared to bring up evidence of a mysterious aquatic world.

Palau is famous for its spectacular and rich coral reefs. But these divers were planning to descend past those sun-lit marine communities and down into a lesser-known twilight zone known as the “mesophotic coral ecosystem.”
Divers prepare to retrieve research structures from down in the “deep reefs.”

highlights.title: 45 Years Ago, a Failed Lord of the Rings Movie Became a Film That Transcended Fantasy
highlights.summary: In the late 15th century, a man named Thomas Malory, whose identity is still debated by scholars, wrote Le Morte d’Arthur, a compilation of legends, chivalric poems, and folklore related to King Arthur and the Knights of the Round Table.
body: As some critics pointed out over the years, Boorman’s epic can throw off spectators with its disjointed flow and weird dialogue. The characters have also been criticized for being inconsistent due to the frequent time jumps in the story, while the plot has been accused of lacking dramatic intensity. However, this is all a result of design rather than incompetence. Excalibur feels more like seeing a stage play than a movie. Every scene is a set piece, a tableau where a fragment of the fairy Arthurian world comes to life. The movie isn’t trying to show a story in the traditional sense. Rather, it attempts something that few works of visual media succeeded at: telling a myth.

Just like myths carry their meaningful symbolism through the ages thanks to powerful images, so Boorman’s ambitious attempt to adapt King Arthur’s tale lives on through the enduring strength of its visuals.

highlights.title: Video Games Europe hits back at EU watchdog targeting King, Supercell, Mojang and more over IAP practices
highlights.summary: The EU’s Consumer Protection Cooperation Network has launched coordinated enforcement actions against games companies including King, Supercell, Mojang, Riot Games, Activision Blizzard and Ubisoft, over how they sell and handle in-game virtual currencies.
body: The CPC Network brings together national consumer protection authorities from across the EU and EEA and is coordinated by the European Commission. In a joint statement published September 30, it said it had found that “a high number of video game companies” had made no substantive changes to their practices since it published non-binding “Key Principles” on in-game currencies in March 2025, despite extensive subsequent talks with industry bodies.

It said the coordinated actions are particularly focused on compliance around variable reward systems such as loot boxes, “dark patterns” and other “harmful influencing techniques”, and practices that directly exhort children to spend money, which it says EU law already prohibits.
Video Games Europe and the European Game Developers Federation pushed back on the CPC Network’s actions in a statement also published on September 30.

highlights.title: Computational tools for society’s most complex challenges
highlights.summary: Associate Professor Cathy Wu uses reinforcement learning to help map out improvements to transportation and other multifaceted systems.
body: As far back as she can remember, Cathy Wu ’12, MNG ’13 wanted to find ways to solve problems to improve people’s lives. Her parents were Taiwanese immigrants, and her father had a long commute to his job, which took him away from the family. On a tight budget, the rest of the family often stayed home on a street that was too busy for playing outdoors. Wu and her siblings ended up playing a lot of computer games.

Wu says her desire to make the world a better place, her dad’s daily battle against traffic, and the games she played, like “SimCity,” were the seeds of her motivation to design safe, efficient transportation systems.

Wu is an associate professor in the MIT Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering (CEE) and the Institute for Data, Systems, and Society (IDSS), and a principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems. Her research focuses on using machine learning and reinforcement learning (RL) to advance reliable strategies for improving a range of complex systems, including transportation.

highlights.title: Deepfake review – ingenious interview with a PM who dances around every issue
highlights.summary: Sadler’s Wells East, London An interrogater tries to get to the bottom of a surreal scandal while green screen actors meddle with the story in Jess and Morgs’ inventive production.
body: What audiences remember most from a political interview, a voiceover tells the prime minister (Kennedy Muntanga) as he prepares to face his TV interrogator (Rebecca Bassett-Graham, coiffed à la Emily Maitlis), is less the words themselves than the tone of voice and the tenor of the body. Muntanga is on point, then: his arms sweep, his fingers beetle and his hands spread out, as if he were wordlessly fielding fly-by questions and offering open statements. It’s the moves and the staging that count.

This setup lands right in the zone for creative duo Jess and Morgs (Jessica Wright and Morgann Runacre-Temple), whose turf is a congenial mix of choreography, film and theatre. In Deepfake, along with writer Jeff James, they explore the various unravellings of an encounter in which the interviewer tries to find the truth behind a surreal – but maybe real? – story in which the PM was seen variously spattered with yellow paint, with his flies undone, and partaking in a ritual involving a deer’s head.

highlights.title: Bailiffs and 100 unpaid teachers: inside the collapse of ‘groundbreaking’ yoga studio Triyoga
highlights.summary: Formerly a favourite of the A-list, the chain has abruptly ceased trading, leaving teachers and customers blindsided. Kate Comer is a single mother with two children, so she is used to living on a financial knife-edge.
body: “I’m just reeling right now,” she said, estimating her loss at about £1,500. “I’m very concerned about the future.”

Comer is one of an estimated 100 yoga teachers who were not paid for their final weeks of teaching before Triyoga, the cult London yoga studio, shut. Several instructors of barre, spin and box-fit classes who taught at its sister brands Barrecore, Boom Cycle, Kobox and Reformcore, which have also closed, have also said they have been left out of pocket.
Yoga teachers who spoke to the Guardian said they felt blindsided by the sudden collapse, and are now struggling to pay essential bills. At least one says they are facing homelessness.

“It’s absolutely disgraceful and there’s nothing we can do about it as freelancers,” said Comer, who is currently going through a divorce and fears that her sudden loss of income will mean she is considered unable to keep the family flat. She is searching for other work, but “the market is saturated with hundreds of teachers”.

highlights.title: Documenting the tech worker movement
highlights.summary: Writing as a participant and researcher, PhD student JS Tan SM ’22 has co-authored a new book about the rise of tech worker protests and the employer backlash that followed.
body: Despite the “dot-com crash” in 2000, the tech industry remained an attractive career destination for many who believed technology represented the future. The digital age — defined by global connectivity and computers — had firmly taken hold, and over time, the tech industry emerged as a dominant force in the labor market. High-paying jobs for engineers, designers, and professionals across a wide range of fields became increasingly common.
MIT PhD student JS Tan SM ’22 was among those who, upon graduating from Brown University and Rhode Island School of Design in 2015, joined the tech industry.
“A lot of us had this idea that technology, and in particular the technologies related to the internet, had the potential for bringing about a more progressive version of the world,” Tan says.
Google echoed this ethos to its employees with its once-famous motto, “don’t be evil,” as their informal corporate philosophy and code of conduct guideline. They’ve since dropped the tagline.

On Friday evening, OpenAI revealed agents had hacked into a New South Wales government website in June and accessed historical non-public data on bushfires without authorisation.

It is the sixth government website in Australia to be notified by the AI giant since last month of agent activity on their services, after the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, announced OpenAI’s agents had hacked into Services Australia’s Medicare statistics portal.

highlights.title: In the footsteps of Wales’s heroic rebel prince: hiking Glyndŵr’s Way
highlights.summary: As Michael Sheen prepares to bring Owain Glyndŵr to life on stage, our writer walks the peaceful national trail named after the last Welsh Prince of Wales. Between the treetops, I can see the towers of a distant mist-shrouded castle.
body: The towers slide away behind trees and a railway viaduct emerges. The medieval castle ruins, it turns out, are believed to have been plundered to build the viaduct in the 1860s, and the builders dropped in a couple of crenelated towers to honour the origins of the stone. I fear this may be an early omen: the spirit of Glyndŵr will be as elusive as the man himself was in his lifetime.

After his great rebellion of 1400 devolved into a murderous guerrilla campaign, the last Welsh prince of Wales simply disappeared. His English adversaries thought he had supernatural powers. Writing two centuries after the events, Shakespeare has Glyndŵr declare (under the anglicised name Owen Glendower) in Henry IV: Part I that “the earth did shake when I was born” and “I can call spirits from the vasty deep”. The last known sighting was in about 1819, when William Blake saw him in a vision and sketched his gaunt head. Since then, nothing. If he’s been hard to pin down for six centuries, what chance now?

When she noticed the email that Saturday night, Kathleen Walters already had far too much going on in her life. Number one was figuring out if the lump in her breast that her doctor had just detected was a tumour. Half of her known blood relatives had died of cancer, and she was now 52: the lump needed understanding.

Whoever had sent this email asking her to list five things she’d done at work was now demanding that all these people inside the IRS share information that, in many cases, should never be shared. She thought it was nuts.

The email came as a surprise, but then the IRS was suddenly full of surprises. Nine days earlier, on 13 February, a Thursday, the first Doge person turned up in the lobby, unannounced, and security called Traci DiMartini, who ran the IRS’s human capital department. There’s a kid down here who said he needs to get into the building, he said. The kid’s name was Gavin Kliger.

highlights.summary: Europe's Consumer Protection Cooperation Network is taking "coordinated actions" against a string of top games companies as it looks to investigate compliance with 'Key Principles' on in-game virtual currencies announced last year.
body: The CPC is a network of national authorities responsible for the enforcement of EU consumer protection laws. It has asked Activision Blizzard, Crytek, InnoGames, King, Mojang, Plarium, PLR Worldwide Sales, Riot Games, Supercell and Ubisoft to bring their commercial practices in line relating to in-game virtual currencies.

Games being assessed include Hunt: Showdown 1896, Forge of Empires, Candy Crush Saga, Minecraft, Mech Arena, Gardenscapes, Valorant, Clash of Clans, For Honor, Diablo Immortal and Call of Duty Mobile.

The games were selected for assessment by the CPC Network "in the context of a wide-scale market compliance check due to broad reach, cross-device accessibility, and varied age ratings, all of which amplify the impact of the practices on consumers".
It's not clear what, if any, 'Key Principles' have not been adhered to prior to the CPC Network opening its investigations.

highlights.title: Tim Dowling: nobody’s laughing – is the joke on me?
highlights.summary: By over-committing to the bit, I’m in danger of becoming the very thing that I mock. There was a kid in my year in high school named Jimmy Tremarelli. We were in a couple of the same classes, and also had occasion to pass each other in the hall between bells about three times a day.
body: Over the years the pretence became gradually more elaborate. Sometimes Jim would steal up alongside me at the end of class, cupping my elbow in the palm of his hand.
“Doctor,” he might say. “I know you’re busy, but I have a case I’d like to get your opinion on.” I would then stare at him gravely for a few seconds.
“Call my secretary,” I would say. Then we’d nod and go our separate ways. We were 15.

I can’t remember how or why it started, but in the hundreds of times Jim and I encountered one another over the course of three years, we never didn’t do it, not once. It wasn’t for anyone else’s benefit – I’m not sure anyone else even knew about it. I just remember students streaming round us, taking no notice as we stood there consulting in the corridor by the gym doors.
points: By over-committing to the bit, I’m in danger of becoming the very thing that I mock.

highlights.title: These AI Experts Want to Do High-Stakes Research Out in the Open
highlights.summary: Many frontier labs keep their risky research locked away. Trillium Labs wants to show off its work when it comes to self-improvement and model behavior.
body: Some big AI companies seem to think that the best way to keep models from becoming too chaotic or too mischievous is to keep them locked inside of labs. If only a chosen few can access them, the thinking goes, they can do less damage in the real world while researchers try to understand what they’re capable of.

Nathan Lambert and Tom Zick, two industry scientists, believe the opposite. The pair founded a nonprofit, Trillium Labs, that will work on various areas of AI research—including potentially problematic areas like recursive self-improvement (RSI) and agents—in a more transparent way. In practice, this will mean publishing the details of experiments so that outside scientists can study and replicate them.

Lambert says the way frontier AI labs keep their work secret reduces the community’s ability to scrutinize ideas and contribute new approaches. He believes that letting outside experts see how models are built and tuned could be crucial to mitigating risks.

highlights.title: Steam Horror Game Turns PS1-Era Graphics Into Backrooms-Style Nightmare Fuel
highlights.summary: There is something uniquely unsettling about empty video game spaces. Blown wide open in the wake of Backrooms, the concept of liminal horror has seeped out from internet forums and chat rooms to become a subculture all its own.
body: It’s a feeling written into the code of some of the greatest PS1 games ever made, from Tomb Raider to Metal Gear Solid. Often born from the limited memory and technical constraints of mid-’90s consoles, such games inadvertently — or deliberately if you’re Silent Hill — turned empty digital spaces into breeding grounds for a sense of unease. This idea would be taken to an even stranger extreme long after the PS1 became a legacy system, thanks to Bryce Bucher’s surreal 2020 horror adventure Fatum Betula. Almost six years after release, it remains one of the clearest examples of how PlayStation-era 3D environments can transform even the emptiest spaces into something deeply unsettling.
